title: Left hand leads
summary: Learn exactly what the left hand's pattern is doing, and make it steady before the tune joins in.
materials: the piece from your teacher, with a pencil

figure.alt: A one-octave keyboard in the left hand's lower register, from C3. C3, E3 and G3 are highlighted as one example broken chord, a shape standing in for the broken chord, walking bass line, or block chords the left-hand pattern might actually be.

steps.title: Left hand leads
steps.body:
The left hand is often the least noticed part of a piece and the most important. A broken chord, a walking bass line, or steady block chords hold the whole piece up. A tune played over a shaky left hand always sounds shaky too.

1. Name what the left-hand pattern actually is: a broken chord, a bass line that moves, or repeated block chords.
2. Play the left hand alone, slowly, until the pattern feels automatic and needs no thinking.
3. Add the right-hand tune on top, slowly, keeping the left hand exactly as steady as it was alone.
4. Play both hands together at tempo, checking that the left hand never sags or rushes under the tune.

A pianist who can play the left hand perfectly alone but loses it once the tune arrives has not learned the left hand yet.

steps.title: Four sittings
steps.body: Fifteen minutes each. Tick a sitting when it is done. Days do not matter; sittings do.
checklist: Sitting 1: name the left-hand pattern, play it alone until automatic
Sitting 2: add the right hand slowly, watching the left hand for sagging
Sitting 3: both hands at tempo, hard bars first if the left hand slips
Sitting 4: the whole piece at tempo, then once as if recording
An old piece played once, listening only to the left hand

steps.title: Record this week's version
steps.prompt: Play the left hand alone once, then play the whole piece with both hands, hands in the frame.
